title: Extreme heat is becoming a public-system resilience problem shaped by urbanization, ageing, communication, and unequal exposure
source_unit: WHO Regional Office for Europe, Heat–health action plans: guidance, second edition
geography: WHO European Region guidance adaptable to national, regional, and local heat-health planning in other contexts

denominator.unit: heat-health risk and public-health planning frame

risk_driver.value: Extreme heat is an urgent and growing public-health threat driven by climate change and exacerbated by urbanization and population ageing

system_load.value: Heat increases morbidity and mortality and strains health and social-care systems

unequal_exposure.value: Populations at increased risk are disproportionately affected

observations.method: WHO Regional Office for Europe guidance synthesizing evidence and implementation experience on heat-health risk prevention, preparedness, response, and learning.
observations.uncertainty: The guidance identifies system risks and actions rather than estimating a universal heat-attributable burden or the effect of any single plan; exposure and vulnerability vary by place and population.
observations.subgroup: Older people, people with chronic illness or disability, outdoor and heat-exposed workers, low-income households, people living alone, urban residents, and people with limited access to cooling or care.
observations.counterinterpretation: Urban and ageing populations can be protected through planning, social connection, cooling, accessible services, and early warning; risk is not determined by age or place alone.

denominator.unit: core elements of WHO heat-health action-plan guidance

governance.value: Governance is one of eight core elements for heat-health action plans

warning_and_surveillance.value: Heat-health warning systems and heat-health surveillance are core elements

resilience_and_exposure.value: Health-system resilience and reducing heat exposure are core elements

learning.value: Monitoring, evaluation, and learning are core elements

observations.method: WHO implementation framework organized around governance, warnings, at-risk populations, communication, health-system resilience, exposure reduction, surveillance, and monitoring and learning.
observations.uncertainty: The presence of a plan or element does not establish implementation quality, reach, public comprehension, reduced exposure, or lower mortality.
observations.subgroup: National, regional, and local authorities; health and social-care systems; emergency services; schools; employers; housing and urban-planning agencies; and communities.
observations.counterinterpretation: A smaller set of well-funded actions may outperform a comprehensive plan that lacks authority, maintenance, staffing, or coordination; formal completeness is not operational readiness.

observations.period: June 2026 guidance; public communication and agency

communication.value: Communication is a core element of heat-health action planning

action_briefs.value: The guidance includes user action briefs for key sectors

message_bank.value: A public-health message bank is provided to support risk communication

observations.method: WHO practical guidance translating heat-health evidence into communication tools, sector-specific actions, and public decision support.
observations.uncertainty: Messages and tools do not guarantee trust, access, behavior change, or protection, especially where housing, work, mobility, language, or care constraints limit feasible action.
observations.subgroup: Residents, caregivers, older people, workers, employers, schools, clinicians, social-care staff, local officials, and people with different languages or communication access.
observations.counterinterpretation: Public messaging can shift responsibility onto individuals when structural conditions—housing quality, energy cost, workplace rules, or service capacity—make recommended actions difficult.

denominator.unit: heat-health planning transfer and adaptation frame

implementation_levels.value: The updated guidance supports action at national, regional, and local levels

adaptability.value: Although tailored to the WHO European Region, the guidance is adaptable to other contexts

coordination.value: Effective heat-health prevention and response require coordinated public-health, social-care, urban, infrastructure, and communication action

observations.method: WHO regional guidance with local, regional, and national decision points and cross-sector implementation tools.
observations.uncertainty: Adaptation across contexts requires local hazard data, institutional authority, funding, cultural fit, and evaluation; transferability is not proof of effectiveness elsewhere.
observations.subgroup: Governments, municipalities, health systems, social-care providers, urban planners, infrastructure operators, employers, civil society, and residents.
observations.counterinterpretation: Central coordination can improve speed and consistency, while local knowledge can improve fit; either level can fail if responsibilities, funding, and accountability are unclear.

related_sources.claim: Complementary WHO 2026 health-workforce evidence on ageing, distribution, and planning capacity.
Complementary child-centred climate, service, and resilience outlook.

boundary: This record adds a heat-health preparedness, urbanization, ageing, care, communication, and cross-sector resilience route. It uses WHO guidance, not a heat-attributable mortality estimate, local plan inventory, individual exposure history, household energy data, causal evaluation, or proof that communication or action plans reduce harm.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official WHO Europe publication page reviewed for the 2026 date, climate/urbanization/ageing risk, health and social-care strain, eight core elements, communication tools, implementation levels, and cross-context adaptability.
